title: Kubernetes and Cloud Native Security Associate (KCSA)

nodes.title: Kubernetes Pod Security Admission: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Pod Security Admission (PSA) replaced PodSecurityPolicy in Kubernetes 1.25+. It enforces three built-in security profiles at the namespace level using labels. CKS exams test the profiles and enforcement modes.

flashcards.back: Privileged (no restrictions), Baseline (prevents known privilege escalations), Restricted (strongly hardened — requires non-root, drops all capabilities, enforces seccompProfile).
enforce (reject violating Pods), audit (log violations but allow), warn (display warning to the user but allow). A namespace can have different levels per mode.

flashcards.front: How to label a namespace for PSA?
flashcards.back: kubectl label namespace <ns> pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted. Add --version=latest to pin the policy version evaluated.
Applies the container runtime's built-in seccomp filter (e.g., Docker's default), which blocks ~300+ dangerous syscalls — required by the Restricted profile.

questions.q: The Kubernetes documentation describes the 'Four Cs of Cloud Native Security' as a defence-in-depth model with four nested layers protecting the application. Which ordering correctly lists the four layers from the outermost layer down to the innermost?
choices: Cluster, then Cloud, then Container, then Code, on the basis that the cluster control plane is the primary trust boundary that the surrounding cloud account ultimately depends on
Container, then Cloud, then Cluster, then Code, since container runtime isolation is enforced by the host kernel before any cloud or cluster control-plane policy is evaluated by the runtime
Code, then Container, then Cluster, then Cloud, reflecting how a typical attacker first compromises application logic and pivots outward toward shared cluster and cloud infrastructure
Cloud, then Cluster, then Container, then Code, where each outer layer establishes the trust boundary that the layer immediately inside it depends on for its own security posture
questions.explanation: The 4Cs are Cloud, Cluster, Container, Code, listed from outermost to innermost. The cloud (or corporate datacentre) is the foundation that the cluster runs on; the cluster sits on the cloud and provides isolation for containers; containers run application code. Each outer layer's security posture directly affects every inner layer, so weaknesses in the cloud or cluster usually cannot be fully compensated for at the container or code layer. Option A inverts cloud and cluster — the cluster is hosted on the cloud, not the other way around. Option B places container outside cloud, which mixes runtime isolation with the trust hierarchy. Option C describes an attacker pivot path, not the nested defence-in-depth layers the documentation defines.

questions.q: A request to create a Pod arrives at the kube-apiserver over TLS. Which sequence correctly describes the stages a successful request passes through inside the API server before the new object is persisted to the cluster datastore?
choices: Authentication, then authorization, then mutating admission, then schema validation, then validating admission, then write to etcd, with each stage able to reject the request entirely

Authorization, then authentication, then schema validation, then mutating admission, then validating admission, then write to etcd, so policy decisions can be cached before the user's identity is verified
Authentication, then mutating admission, then validating admission, then authorization, then schema validation, then write to etcd, so admission webhooks see every request regardless of RBAC
Authentication, then authorization, then schema validation, then validating admission, then mutating admission, then write to etcd, ensuring validators never see partially mutated objects on the wire
questions.explanation: The kube-apiserver pipeline for a write is: authentication (who are you), authorization (are you allowed), mutating admission (webhooks may modify the object), schema validation (does it match the API schema), validating admission (final policy checks), then persistence to etcd. Option B reverses authn/authz — authorization needs the verified identity to make a decision and cannot precede authentication. Option C bypasses RBAC by running admission before authorization, which would let unauthorised callers exercise webhooks. Option D places mutating after validating, which would let mutating webhooks change an object that has already been validated, defeating the purpose of validation.

questions.q: A security review of a production cluster examines how etcd is deployed. Which configuration most directly mitigates the risk that an attacker who reaches etcd over the network can read or modify any cluster object?
choices: Expose etcd through a ClusterIP Service so only Pods can reach it, and rely on a default-deny NetworkPolicy in kube-system to bound the blast radius of any reachable etcd endpoint
Replace etcd's native authentication with the same OIDC provider used by the API server, so end-user identities flow end-to-end through every layer of the control plane on every cluster request
Run etcd inside a privileged Pod with hostNetwork: true, audit every kubectl exec against that Pod, and rely on the kube-apiserver to perform application-level encryption on every write to etcd
Require mutual TLS between etcd peers and clients, issue narrowly scoped client certificates to the API server only, and place the etcd nodes on a private network unreachable from workloads
questions.explanation: etcd holds the entire cluster state, including Secrets. Production deployments must require mutual TLS on both peer and client endpoints, restrict client certificates to the kube-apiserver identity, and isolate etcd on a private network not reachable from workload nodes. Option A is the opposite — putting etcd behind a ClusterIP makes it reachable from every Pod, and NetworkPolicy is not a substitute for mTLS or network isolation of the datastore. Option B is wrong because etcd does not delegate authentication to OIDC and end-user identities should never reach etcd; only the API server should. Option C runs etcd in a privileged Pod with host networking, which widens host exposure rather than reducing it.

questions.q: A namespace carries the label `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted`. A user submits a Pod whose container sets `securityContext.runAsUser: 0` and `securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation: true`. What does Pod Security Admission do at admission time?
choices: Rejects the Pod creation request, because the restricted profile forbids running as UID 0 and explicitly disallows `allowPrivilegeEscalation: true` on every container in any Pod in that namespace
Logs a warning event, admits the Pod into the namespace, and triggers a runtime alert only if the container later attempts a syscall that is blocked by the restricted seccomp profile in use
Mutates the Pod to set `runAsNonRoot: true` and `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`, then admits the resulting object so that the workload can still be created without any manual edits at all
Admits the Pod but assigns it to a separate RuntimeClass whose AppArmor profile is treated as an automatic compensating control for the disallowed fields in the container's securityContext
questions.explanation: Pod Security Admission is a validating-only admission controller. With `enforce: restricted`, Pods that violate the restricted profile — including running as UID 0 or allowing privilege escalation — are rejected at admission time. Option B confuses admission control with runtime detection: PSA decides before the Pod is created, not based on later syscalls. Option C is wrong because PSA never mutates Pods; the spec must be fixed by the submitter (set `runAsNonRoot: true`, `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`, drop all capabilities, set a seccomp profile). Option D is fabricated — PSA does not assign RuntimeClasses or apply AppArmor profiles as compensating controls.

questions.q: A Pod in namespace `web` is not selected by any NetworkPolicy in its namespace, and the cluster's CNI plugin fully implements NetworkPolicy. What ingress traffic does this Pod accept?
choices: Only traffic from Pods in the same namespace, because Kubernetes applies an implicit cluster-wide policy that permits same-namespace traffic and blocks everything else by default
No ingress traffic from any source, because Pods that are not selected by any NetworkPolicy default to deny-all in Kubernetes regardless of which CNI plugin happens to be installed
All ingress traffic, because in Kubernetes a Pod that is not selected by any NetworkPolicy has no traffic restrictions applied and the cluster network is open by default to any source
Only traffic that matches an auto-generated policy mirroring the Pod's Service selector, so flows arriving via the Service ClusterIP are permitted but direct Pod-IP sources are denied
questions.explanation: Kubernetes networking is open by default. A NetworkPolicy only takes effect on Pods that match its `podSelector`. As soon as one or more policies select a Pod, the Pod becomes isolated for the matched directions and only flows explicitly allowed by any selecting policy are permitted. A Pod that is no policy's subject remains fully reachable. Option A is wrong because Kubernetes ships no implicit same-namespace policy. Option B inverts the actual default — there is no built-in deny-all; a deny-all policy must be created explicitly. Option D is fabricated — Kubernetes does not auto-generate NetworkPolicies from Service selectors, and Service routing does not translate into per-Pod ingress allowances.

questions.q: A cluster has a Role `pod-reader` in namespace `app` granting `get`, `list`, and `watch` on `pods`. ServiceAccount `app-sa` in `app` is bound to this Role via a RoleBinding. The same ServiceAccount is also the subject of a ClusterRoleBinding to a ClusterRole `pod-reader-cluster` with the same verbs on `pods`. Where can `app-sa` list Pods?
choices: Only in the `app` namespace, because a RoleBinding to a ServiceAccount always shadows any ClusterRoleBinding that grants the same verbs to the same subject
Only in the namespace where the ServiceAccount object lives, because a ClusterRoleBinding's reach is bounded by the subject's home namespace when the subject is a ServiceAccount
In every namespace and at cluster scope where the listed verbs apply, because a ClusterRoleBinding grants its ClusterRole's permissions to the subject across the entire cluster
In every namespace except `kube-system`, because system namespaces are exempt from cross-namespace permissions granted to non-system ServiceAccounts by a ClusterRoleBinding
questions.explanation: RBAC is purely additive. A RoleBinding grants its Role's permissions inside the binding's namespace; a ClusterRoleBinding grants the bound ClusterRole's permissions across the entire cluster for the subject. The two bindings stack rather than conflict, so `app-sa` can list Pods in any namespace. Option A invents a 'shadowing' rule — RBAC never subtracts; it only adds. Option B is wrong because a ClusterRoleBinding's reach is the whole cluster regardless of where the subject ServiceAccount lives. Option D fabricates a `kube-system` exemption that does not exist in RBAC.

nodes.title: Software supply-chain security: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Software supply-chain security protects everything that goes into building and delivering software — third-party dependencies, build pipelines, and published artifacts — because attackers increasingly compromise the supply chain instead of the app directly. Exams cover SBOMs, dependency risk, signing and provenance, and pipeline hardening.

flashcards.back: A Software Bill of Materials — a complete inventory of every component, library, and dependency in a piece of software, including versions. It lets you quickly answer 'are we affected?' when a new vulnerability (like Log4Shell) drops, instead of guessing what's inside your builds.

flashcards.front: What are typosquatting and poisoned dependencies?
flashcards.back: Typosquatting publishes a malicious package with a name nearly identical to a popular one (e.g., a one-letter difference), hoping you install it by mistake. A poisoned dependency is a legitimate package that's been compromised to inject malicious code into everyone who pulls it. Both attack you through trusted package ecosystems.

flashcards.front: What do artifact signing and provenance provide?
flashcards.back: Signing (e.g., with Sigstore/cosign) cryptographically proves an artifact came from a trusted publisher and wasn't tampered with. Provenance is verifiable metadata about how and where an artifact was built. Frameworks like SLSA define maturity levels for trustworthy, tamper-resistant build pipelines.

flashcards.front: How do you secure the CI/CD pipeline itself?
flashcards.back: Treat the pipeline as a high-value target: lock down build runners, scope credentials to least privilege and prefer short-lived tokens over stored secrets, pin and verify dependencies, isolate build steps, and require code review. A compromised build server can sign and ship malware as if it were legitimate.

questions.q: During a threat-model exercise the team reviews Pod spec patterns that materially expand the blast radius of a compromised container. Which configuration most directly enables a process inside the Pod to read or modify files on the underlying node's filesystem?
choices: Requesting more CPU than the node currently has free, which forces the kubelet to map sensitive scheduling pages from the host kernel into the Pod's memory space until pressure subsides
Setting `imagePullPolicy: Always` so every restart re-pulls the image, which opens a brief window during which container isolation is intentionally relaxed by the runtime for layer extraction
Mounting a `hostPath` volume that points at a sensitive node directory such as `/`, `/etc`, or `/var/run/docker.sock`, and exposing that mount inside the container with read/write permissions

Selecting `restartPolicy: OnFailure` together with a `livenessProbe` of type `exec`, which causes the kubelet to bind-mount the node's binary directory into the container so the probe command resolves
questions.explanation: A `hostPath` volume mounts a path from the node directly into the container, which lets a compromised process read or modify node files. Pointing it at `/`, `/etc`, or a runtime socket effectively breaks the container/node boundary and is a classic node-escape primitive. Option A is fabricated — CPU pressure causes scheduling failures or throttling, never an exposure of host memory. Option B is wrong because `imagePullPolicy` controls when images are pulled, not isolation guarantees; the runtime never relaxes isolation during image extraction. Option D is invented — `livenessProbe: exec` runs inside the container's existing mount namespace and the kubelet does not bind-mount node binaries.

questions.q: A platform team wants the cluster to admit only container images that carry a valid cryptographic signature and an SLSA-style provenance attestation. Which combination of tools most directly delivers this control at admission time?
choices: Trivy scanning images during the CI build and failing the pipeline on critical CVEs, with the same scan report attached to the image so the kubelet can read it before allowing the container to start
Notary v1 trust pinning configured in the kubelet via `imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent`, so the runtime refuses to pull any image whose canonical name does not already include a fixed content digest
A private container registry served over TLS, plus a custom MutatingWebhook that downloads each requested image, recomputes its SHA-256 digest, and patches the Pod spec inline with the result

Sigstore Cosign to sign images and attach in-toto/SLSA attestations, paired with a policy engine such as Kyverno or Sigstore Policy Controller that verifies the signature and attestations at admission
questions.explanation: Cosign (part of the Sigstore project) signs images and attaches in-toto attestations such as SLSA provenance. An admission-time policy engine like Kyverno or Sigstore's Policy Controller verifies those signatures and attestations against trusted keys or identities before admitting the Pod. Option A is wrong because Trivy is a vulnerability scanner — it does not sign images or produce SLSA attestations, and the kubelet does not read CVE reports at admission. Option B confuses Notary v1 / Docker Content Trust with kubelet behaviour: the kubelet does not implement Notary trust pinning, and `imagePullPolicy` controls caching, not trust. Option C only proves a digest matches itself; recomputing a hash does not verify a signer's intent.

questions.q: A workload reads database credentials from a Kubernetes Secret mounted as a volume. The cluster runs with default settings and no `EncryptionConfiguration` is configured on the API server. Which statement about the confidentiality of these credentials is correct?
choices: The Secret value is only base64-encoded in etcd and is stored as plaintext from a confidentiality standpoint, so anyone who can read etcd directly can recover the credentials without keys
The Secret value is hashed with SHA-256 before being written to etcd, so only the workload that originally created the Secret can recover the plaintext on read by presenting the matching pre-image
The Secret value is encrypted at rest by default using a per-cluster data encryption key, which the API server unwraps with the cluster root key on every read from etcd before returning it to clients

The Secret value is automatically replaced with a reference to a managed KMS entry by the API server, and only an opaque ciphertext blob ever reaches the etcd datastore on disk in this default configuration
questions.explanation: By default Kubernetes Secrets are stored in etcd as base64-encoded data, which is encoding, not encryption. Anyone with read access to etcd (or to an etcd backup) can recover the plaintext. To get encryption at rest, the cluster operator must configure `EncryptionConfiguration` on the API server, typically using a KMS provider. Option B is wrong because hashing is one-way and the workload would never be able to retrieve the plaintext from a hash. Option C describes the encryption-at-rest feature but it is opt-in, not on by default; a stock cluster has no such DEK in place. Option D is fabricated — the API server does not push Secrets to an external KMS automatically; that integration must be explicitly configured.

questions.q: A new auditor asks how the cluster maps to recognized hardening baselines. Which statement most accurately describes the CIS Kubernetes Benchmark?
choices: A NIST-published compliance regulation that imposes legally binding hardening requirements on Kubernetes clusters operating in regulated industries, enforced through federal audit programmes

A community-maintained, consensus-based set of hardening recommendations covering control-plane and worker-node configuration, widely used as a reference checklist for assessing Kubernetes security posture
A runtime-only set of eBPF detection rules distributed by the CNCF that flags suspicious container syscalls at execution time but does not offer guidance about cluster configuration choices or RBAC
A formal certification programme managed by the Linux Foundation that a cluster must pass before any vendor is allowed to use the upstream Kubernetes name or trademark in their marketing materials
questions.explanation: The CIS Kubernetes Benchmark is a consensus-based document published by the Center for Internet Security with prescriptive hardening recommendations for both the control plane and worker nodes. Auditors and tools such as `kube-bench` use it as a reference checklist. Option A misattributes the document to NIST and treats it as legally binding — it is neither. Option C describes Falco-style runtime detection, which is not the CIS Benchmark's purpose. Option D conflates it with the CNCF Certified Kubernetes Conformance programme, which governs trademark use but is unrelated to security hardening.

questions.q: A workload does not call the Kubernetes API at all, yet by default its Pod is given a mounted ServiceAccount token. Which configuration most directly reduces the risk that a compromised container reuses that token against the API server?
choices: Set `automountServiceAccountToken: false` on the Pod (or its ServiceAccount) so no API token is projected into the container, removing a credential an attacker could otherwise reuse
Bind the Pod's ServiceAccount to a ClusterRole that grants `get` on `secrets` cluster-wide, so the workload always retrieves credentials freshly from etcd rather than relying on the projected token
Mount the default token but set `imagePullPolicy: Always`, ensuring the container image is re-pulled each restart so any tampered token baked into a layer is overwritten on boot
Run the Pod with `hostNetwork: true` so its API calls originate from the node IP, letting a NetworkPolicy on the node interface block the token from ever reaching the API server
questions.explanation: If a workload never calls the API, the safest control is to stop projecting a token at all via `automountServiceAccountToken: false`, eliminating a credential an attacker could steal and replay. Option B is the opposite of least privilege: granting cluster-wide read on Secrets massively widens the blast radius if the Pod is compromised, and the projected token is still mounted. Option C is irrelevant — tokens are not baked into image layers; they are dynamically projected at Pod start, so `imagePullPolicy` has no effect on token presence. Option D is wrong because `hostNetwork: true` does not interpose a NetworkPolicy choke point on the kubelet's interface and would actually broaden the Pod's network exposure.

questions.q: A security team wants runtime detection that flags suspicious behavior inside running containers — such as a shell spawned in a container or an unexpected write to `/etc` — by observing Linux syscalls. Which CNCF project is purpose-built for this runtime threat-detection use case?
choices: Kyverno, a policy engine that intercepts API requests at admission and rejects or mutates Pods, providing equivalent coverage to syscall-level monitoring because every action passes through the API server first
Falco, a runtime security project that consumes kernel syscall events via eBPF or a kernel module and raises alerts when container behaviour matches rules such as a shell spawning in a container
Trivy, a scanner that surfaces suspicious runtime behaviours by analysing the container image's layers and software bill of materials before the workload is ever scheduled onto a node
cert-manager, which issues and rotates workload certificates and additionally watches syscall activity to detect when a compromised process attempts to exfiltrate a private key at runtime
questions.explanation: Falco is the CNCF runtime security tool that ingests kernel syscall events through eBPF or a kernel module and alerts on suspicious behaviour like an interactive shell in a container or writes to sensitive paths. Option A confuses admission control with runtime observation: Kyverno can reject a Pod spec at admission but cannot see syscalls once the container is running. Option C is wrong because Trivy is a static scanner of images and SBOMs; it runs before execution and cannot observe runtime behaviour. Option D fabricates a feature — cert-manager only handles certificate lifecycle; it has no syscall-monitoring capability.

nodes.title: Compliance frameworks: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Compliance is the discipline of mapping your controls to an external framework (PCI, HIPAA, SOC 2, GDPR, ISO 27001) and proving it to an auditor. Most exam questions test which framework owns which scope, not the minutiae of each clause.

flashcards.back: Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard. Applies to anyone who stores, processes, or transmits cardholder data (PAN, expiry, CVV). 12 high-level requirements: firewalls, no defaults, encrypted storage, encrypted transmission, antivirus, secure dev, restrict access, MFA, log, test, policy. Required by Visa/Mastercard, not by law.

flashcards.front: HIPAA vs HITRUST — what's the difference?
flashcards.back: HIPAA is U.S. law for protected health information (PHI) — sets the legal requirements but is high-level on technical controls. HITRUST CSF is a certifiable framework that operationalizes HIPAA (plus ISO, NIST, PCI) into specific testable controls. Healthcare orgs are legally HIPAA-bound; many also pursue HITRUST cert to prove diligence.

American Institute of CPAs report on a SaaS company's controls across five trust criteria: security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, privacy. Type I = controls designed at a point in time. Type II = controls operated effectively over 6-12 months. Enterprise customers ask for the Type II as proof you're not making it up.

flashcards.front: GDPR — what does it require beyond US-style privacy laws?
flashcards.back: European General Data Protection Regulation. Requires explicit consent (not pre-ticked), right to access / deletion / portability, 72-hour breach notification, data protection officer (for large processors), data minimization, and Privacy Impact Assessments for high-risk processing. Fines: up to 4% of global revenue. Applies to anyone processing EU residents' data, regardless of company location.

questions.q: An attacker who obtains a low-privilege foothold in a Pod attempts to escalate by abusing the kubelet. Which kubelet configuration most directly limits an attacker's ability to call the kubelet API to read Secrets-bearing Pods or exec into containers on that node?
choices: Enable `--anonymous-auth=true` on the kubelet so every request carries an explicit `system:anonymous` identity, which the API server then maps to a ServiceAccount before the kubelet authorizes the call

Set the kubelet's `--authorization-mode=AlwaysAllow` and rely on the API server's RBAC to retroactively reject any kubelet call that a Pod's ServiceAccount was not permitted to make against the cluster
Expose the kubelet's read-only port 10255 to the Pod network so monitoring agents can scrape it, and disable the authenticated port 10250 to remove the surface an attacker would otherwise target
Configure the kubelet with `--anonymous-auth=false` and `--authorization-mode=Webhook` so unauthenticated requests are rejected and authenticated ones are checked against the API server's authorizer
questions.explanation: Hardening the kubelet means disabling anonymous access (`--anonymous-auth=false`) and delegating authorization to the API server (`--authorization-mode=Webhook`), so only authenticated, authorized callers can hit the kubelet API. Option A is the opposite — `--anonymous-auth=true` accepts unauthenticated requests and does not magically map them to a ServiceAccount. Option B disables kubelet authorization entirely; `AlwaysAllow` permits every call that reaches the kubelet regardless of API-server RBAC, which is not retroactively consulted. Option C is dangerous because port 10255 exposes Pod data without authentication, and disabling the authenticated port 10250 breaks kube-apiserver-to-kubelet calls that the cluster depends on.

questions.q: A team wants its container images to minimize the attack surface available to an attacker who achieves code execution inside the container. Which image-construction practice most directly supports this goal?
choices: Base every image on a full general-purpose distribution and install a shell, package manager, and debugging tools so incident responders can investigate in place, accepting the larger footprint as a tradeoff
Build minimal or distroless images that contain only the application and its runtime dependencies, omitting shells and package managers so a compromised process has far fewer tools to abuse

Always pull images by the mutable `latest` tag so the runtime fetches the newest build on every restart, ensuring the running container can never lag behind upstream security fixes pushed to the registry

Run every container as UID 0 inside the image so file permissions never block the application, then rely on the node's default seccomp profile alone to contain any post-exploitation activity attempted
questions.explanation: Minimal or distroless images ship only the app and its runtime libraries, removing shells, package managers, and utilities — so an attacker who lands code execution has very few tools to escalate or pivot. Option A bundles a shell and full toolchain, which directly enlarges the attack surface that minimisation is meant to shrink. Option C is wrong because the mutable `latest` tag undermines reproducibility and supply-chain integrity; security teams pin by content digest instead, and 'newest' is not synonymous with 'patched'. Option D maximises in-container privilege; the default seccomp profile is not a substitute for non-root execution and a minimal image.

questions.q: While threat-modeling the cluster, the team classifies the danger that a low-privileged workload steals a more privileged ServiceAccount token and uses it to act against the API server. Which threat category from the STRIDE model does this scenario best illustrate?
choices: Repudiation, because the attacker performs actions that cannot later be attributed to any identity, defeating the cluster's audit logging rather than gaining any additional authority on the API
Denial of Service, because consuming another workload's token exhausts the API server's authentication capacity and prevents legitimate ServiceAccounts from completing their own requests on time
Elevation of Privilege, because the attacker acquires and reuses a more privileged credential to perform API actions that exceed the rights of the workload they originally compromised
Tampering, because the act of reading another Pod's projected token modifies the token's stored value in etcd and corrupts the cluster's record of which ServiceAccount the credential belongs to
questions.explanation: Stealing and reusing a more privileged token to act beyond one's original rights is the definition of Elevation of Privilege in STRIDE. Option A confuses identity gain with attribution loss — repudiation concerns denying actions one performed, not acquiring new authority. Option B is wrong because token reuse does not consume the API server's authentication capacity; the API server validates tokens cheaply and one workload's misuse does not starve another. Option D mischaracterises a read as a write — projected tokens are read by the compromised Pod, not modified in etcd, so no tampering occurs.

questions.q: A regulated organization must demonstrate that its workloads handle personal data in line with a recognized framework, and it wants Kubernetes-native, continuous evidence that policies are enforced rather than a one-time manual review. Which approach best fits this compliance objective?
choices: Run a manual penetration test once per year and archive the resulting PDF report, treating the absence of findings as continuous proof that the cluster's data-handling controls remain compliant over time
Adopt policy-as-code with an admission engine such as Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper, paired with periodic configuration scanning so controls are enforced at admission and continuously audited
Set the namespace label `compliance: true` on every namespace holding personal data, which signals to the API server that those namespaces are exempt from further policy enforcement obligations
Disable audit logging to reduce the volume of personal data the cluster retains, on the basis that holding fewer records is the most direct way to satisfy any data-protection framework's requirements
questions.explanation: Continuous, Kubernetes-native compliance is achieved with policy-as-code: an admission engine like Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper enforces required controls at admission, and periodic configuration scanning continuously audits posture against the framework. Option A provides only point-in-time evidence and confuses absence of findings with active enforcement. Option C is fabricated — the `compliance: true` label has no built-in meaning to the API server and grants no exemption. Option D removes the very audit trail that frameworks like GDPR, HIPAA, and PCI DSS require as evidence of control operation; it weakens compliance rather than satisfying it.
